steps.text: For a closed point $x$ in an affine open $U$, choose ideals of $X\setminus U$ and $(X\setminus U)\cup\{x\}$. Their quotient is the residue field at $x$. Zero first cohomology lifts its element $1$ to a global function $f$ with $x\in X_f\subset U$.

Each $X_f=D(f|_U)$ is affine. These opens contain all closed points. A nonempty closed complement in the quasi-compact space would have a closed point, so the opens cover $X$. Keep finitely many functions $f_1,\ldots,f_n$.

The map $O_X^n\to O_X$ with entries $f_i$ is surjective on stalks. Its kernel has a finite filtration whose factors are quasi-coherent ideals. Long exact sequences give zero first cohomology of the kernel, so there are global $a_i$ with $\sum a_if_i=1$.

The principal opens $X_{f_i}$ are affine and their functions generate the unit ideal in $A=\Gamma(X,O_X)$. Localization identifies each with $\operatorname{Spec}A_{f_i}$. These identifications agree on intersections and glue to $X\cong\operatorname{Spec}A$.

source.excerpt: Lemma 30.4.5 . Let $f : X \to S$ be a morphism of schemes. Assume that $f$ is quasi-separated and quasi-compact. For any quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_ X$-module $\mathcal{F}$ the higher direct images $R^ pf_*\mathcal{F}$ are quasi-coherent on $S$. If $S$ is quasi-compact, there exists an integer $n = n(X, S, f)$ such that $R^ pf_*\mathcal{F} = 0$ for all $p \geq n$ and any quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ on $X$. In fact, if $S$ is quasi-compact we can find $n = n(X, S, f)$ such that for every morphism of schemes $S' \to S$ we have $R^ p(f')_*\mathcal{F}' = 0$ for $p \geq n$ and any quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}'$ on $X'$. Here $f' : X' = S' \times _ S X \to S'$ is the base change of $f$.

steps.text: Higher direct images commute with restriction to base opens. Quasi-coherence is local on the base. We can therefore assume $S$ affine and $X$ quasi-compact and quasi-separated.
For an affine open $U\subset X$, the map $U\to S$ is affine. Its degree-zero pushforward is quasi-coherent, and all positive higher direct images vanish by affine vanishing.

For a union $U\cup V$, relative Mayer-Vietoris expresses each higher direct image as an extension of a kernel and a cokernel of the direct images on $U,V,U\cap V$. Quasi-coherent sheaves form an abelian category. The quasi-compact open induction principle completes the proof.

source.excerpt: Lemma 30.16.1 . Let $R$ be a Noetherian ring. Let $X \to \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(R)$ be a proper morphism. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be an ample invertible sheaf on $X$. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a coherent $\mathcal{O}_ X$-module. The graded ring $A = \bigoplus _{d \geq 0} H^0(X, \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d})$ is a finitely generated $R$-algebra. There exists an $r \geq 0$ and $d_1, \ldots , d_ r \in \mathbf{Z}$ and a surjection \[ \bigoplus \nolimits _{j = 1, \ldots , r} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d_ j} \longrightarrow \mathcal{F}. \] For any $p$ the cohomology group $H^ p(X, \mathcal{F})$ is a finite $R$-module. If $p > 0$, then $H^ p(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes _{\mathcal{O}_ X} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}) = 0$ for all $d$ large enough. For any $k \in \mathbf{Z}$ the graded $A$-module \[ \bigoplus \nolimits _{d \geq k} H^0(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes _{\mathcal{O}_ X} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}) \] is a finite $A$-module.

steps.text: The published construction chooses finitely many affine opens meeting every generic point. Their intersection U is dense. Replace X by the scheme-theoretic closure of U if needed, which preserves surjectivity and the isomorphism over U.
Embed each affine chart into a projective space over S, then take the closure of the diagonal copy of U in their product. The projections to the chart closures are proper.

steps.why: Lemma 30.21.3 extends sections of sufficiently high powers near y. Morphisms Lemmas 29.40.4 and 29.42.7 give the closed immersion from fiber ampleness.

Properness gives a finite affine cover and separatedness gives affine intersections. Čech comparison computes cohomology. Relative sheaf flatness gives flat section modules. The alternating complex has finitely many degrees.
Tensor gives the pullback module on each affine intersection. These identifications respect restriction maps. A bounded complex of flat modules computes derived tensor for every A-algebra B.

Proper coherence gives finite cohomology. Boundedness gives pseudo-coherence over Noetherian A. A⊕M splits as A-modules. Thus tensor with M has uniformly bounded cohomology. Lemma 15.76.2 gives perfection.
Lemma 37.53.1 gives the integral relative spectrum and the identity for g_*O_X. Lemmas 26.21.13 and 29.15.8 give separatedness and finite type. Universal closedness then gives properness.
Cohomology of Schemes Lemma 30.5.2 preserves global functions under flat étale base change. Lemma 37.53.3 reduces geometric connectedness to connectedness after these pointed étale extensions.

Lemma 36.32.7 makes each fiber idempotent the image of a base element after localization. The map factors through the residue field. Nonempty fibers make this field map injective. Thus only 0 and 1 occur.
For every test scheme the kernel consists exactly of units with nth power 1. This is the definition of μ_n. Its inclusion is injective.
The monic polynomial gives the basis 1 through T^(n−1). Positive rank makes B faithfully flat. The element a^(-1)T^(n−1) is the inverse of T.
Both n and T are units. The derivative criterion gives an étale map. Faithful flatness gives surjectivity. Affine root covers cover arbitrary test schemes and supply nth roots on both sites.

Theorem 59.45.2 is the real published ingredient. It gives equivalence of étale objects under universal homeomorphisms. Integrality and radiciality supply more information than an ordinary homeomorphism.
Universal homeomorphisms remain surjective after each base change. A family covers an étale object exactly when its pullback covers. Thus the category equivalence preserves the topology.

An equivalence of abelian sheaf categories is exact and preserves injectives. It identifies terminal objects and global sections. Corresponding injective resolutions therefore give identical cohomology in every nonnegative degree.

computations.why: The spectrum is Noetherian and the morphism is proper. The line bundle is ample on the specified closed fiber. The theorem therefore gives V.

Since Y=D(a)⊆V⊆Y the neighborhood equals Y. The relative ampleness conclusion therefore holds over the whole local base.
Projective space is flat and proper over A. A locally free sheaf on this flat scheme is flat over A. The line bundle is coherent.
The standard affine cover gives H^0=0. The degree-1 quotient A[t,t^(-1)]/(A[t]+t^(-2)A[t^(-1)]) has basis t^(-1). Higher degrees vanish.
The complex is A in degree 1 up to quasi-isomorphism. Since A is free its derived tensor is B in degree 1. The same Laurent calculation over B agrees.
Each projective-line structure map has pushforward O equal to O_S over every affine base open. Sections on the disjoint union form the product algebra.
The 2 complementary idempotents split the relative spectrum into 2 copies of S. The algebra is locally free of rank 2. Hence the map is finite.
The natural map sends each projective line to its corresponding copy of S. Every geometric fiber is a projective line over an algebraically closed field and is connected.
The polynomial T^2+1 is irreducible over R. Evaluation at i identifies its quotient with C.
In C the element 2T has inverse −T/2. The derivative criterion gives étaleness. The degree-2 field extension gives a surjective spectrum map.
Every real square is nonnegative so −1 has no real square root. In C the unit i satisfies i^2=−1. This supplies the required local root.
The quotient k[ε]/(ε^2)→k has kernel (ε). Its square is zero. The induced spectrum map is a closed immersion.
Every base change gives a closed immersion with square-zero defining ideal. Every prime contains a nilpotent ideal. Thus each changed immersion is a homeomorphism.
The immersion is a universal homeomorphism by a2. The theorem therefore identifies cohomology with that of the restricted abelian sheaf for every q≥0.

steps.why: The residue field is separably closed so the étale point has the same residue field. The henselian splitting theorem gives the R factor and therefore an S-section through the chosen point.

Every pointed neighbourhood receives a pointed map from S. Such a map is unique since sections of an étale morphism that agree at the closed point agree on the local scheme. Thus the stalk colimit is F(S).
Geometric stalks preserve exact sequences of abelian sheaves. The identification makes global sections exact and an exact functor has zero positive right derived functors.

In characteristic p the map t to t^p-t is additive. Its roots for a equal to zero form the constant F_p sheaf. The root algebra for general a is finite free of rank p and étale because the derivative is -1; it is a surjective cover.
The structure sheaf is quasi-coherent. The supplied source names the étale-Zariski comparison theorem and affine vanishing; together they make every positive étale cohomology group of O_X zero.
The long exact sequence has H^(q-1)(O_X) mapping to H^q(F_p) and then to H^q(O_X). Both outside groups vanish for q at least 2. For q equal to 1 the cokernel of F-1 on global sections can survive.

On each regular curve component the local rings at closed points are discrete valuation rings. A rational function with all valuations zero is a unit and each local divisor has a local parameter. This gives the stated sheaf sequence with all generic points understood.

computations.why: The ring k[[t]] is complete local and therefore henselian. Its residue field is k; algebraic closure implies separable closure. Thus it is strictly henselian.
The geometric stalk of the constant sheaf Z/n is Z/n. As usual n must be a positive integer; invertibility of n is not needed here.
The stalk identification gives H^0 equal to Z/n. Exact global sections on this strictly henselian local scheme give zero in every positive degree.
The Artin-Schreier long exact sequence and H^1(X,O_X) equal to zero identify H^1(X,F_p) with the additive cokernel of b to b^p-b on k[t].
A nonconstant polynomial b of degree m has b^p-b of degree pm since pm exceeds m. A constant b gives a constant. Neither case gives t of degree one; its class is nonzero.
The affine line is affine of characteristic p. The theorem therefore kills every degree at least 2 despite the nonzero degree-one class.
The projective line is smooth of dimension one over k. Algebraic closure of k satisfies the remaining hypothesis and gives H^2(X,G_m) equal to zero.
By definition the cohomological Brauer group is the torsion subgroup of H^2_et(X,G_m). This does not require an identification with Azumaya algebras.
The torsion subgroup of the zero group is zero. Independently degree gives Pic(P^1_k) isomorphic to Z with generator O(1); degree-one cohomology need not vanish.
Affine space of relative dimension one is smooth over its base. Localization at ell makes ell a unit on Spec Z[1/ell]; take ell to be a positive integer.
Every element of the constant abelian sheaf Z/ell has order dividing the invertible integer ell. The fibre product of A^1_S with T is A^1_T.

The square is cartesian and g has the required quasi-compactness and quasi-separatedness. Pullback preserves the constant sheaf Z/ell so smooth base change gives the stated comparison for every nonnegative q.
The polynomial ring k[x,y] is a finitely generated k-algebra of Krull dimension two. Its spectrum is affine of finite type.
An algebraically closed field has trivial absolute Galois group. Its étale global-section functor is exact so all positive torsion cohomology groups vanish and its cohomological dimension is zero.
Substitution gives cd(A^2_k) at most 2+0. By the torsion-sheaf definition this kills H^q_et(X,F) for every torsion abelian sheaf F and every q greater than 2.
